w: Five pavilions raised in 1924-1930 by re-erecting salvaged steel frames from German First World War Zeppelin hangars shipped from a Courland airfield, still holding their airship curve. Dairy, meat, fish and vegetable halls ring a UNESCO-listed square that has traded daily since 1930, once Europe's largest market.
s: Zeppelin hangars turned market halls
why: Its five giant pavilions are genuine World War One airship hangars, repurposed rather than replicated.

w: Amber, leather and woodcarvings still change hands under the same Renaissance arcades where medieval merchants sold cloth by royal decree. Rebuilt after a 1555 fire gutted the 14th-century original, its attic once held a fire brigade and now houses the National Museum's 19th-century Polish gallery.
s: Renaissance cloth hall still trading, 700 years on
why: One of the oldest continuously operating commercial buildings in Europe, at the centre of a UNESCO World Heritage square.

w: Vienna's cart traders have sold produce here since the 1780s, when it was a dairy market beside the Wien river; the name, roughly 'nibble market', stuck by around 1820. Otto Wagner's 1916 wartime pavilions still stand over stalls selling Balkan cheese, Turkish spices and sauerkraut by the barrel.
s: Vienna's 18th-century nibble market
why: The city's oldest and largest market, laid out over a culverted river and still run by long-standing trading families.

w: Arabic in name, from a phrase meaning place of the fair, and Arab in rhythm, this street market has run through Albergheria since at least the 10th century. Abbanniata vendors still cry prices over swordfish heads, prickly pears and fried panelle, the layout barely changed since Bourbon-era arcades went up.
s: A thousand years of Arab-Sicilian street trading
why: One of Palermo's oldest markets, its Arabic-derived name and street cries preserving a millennium of trading culture.

w: Antique dealers and ragpickers have traded here since medieval times, when the fair sat by Sant Jaume church before shifting stalls across the city for six centuries. Since 2013 the same jumble of furniture, vinyl and bric-a-brac has spread beneath a vast mirrored steel canopy near Placa de les Glories.
s: 700-year-old flea market under a mirrored roof
why: Barcelona's oldest flea market, tracing an unbroken lineage back to a 14th-century fair.

w: Seven hundred shops once crowded this stretch of Red Square before Alexander Pomerantsev roofed three parallel arcades in glass and iron in 1893, hiding a steel skeleton behind pseudo-Russian facades. Nationalised, then turned into Five Year Plan offices under Stalin, it reopened as a showcase department store in 1953.
s: Tsarist arcades that outlasted Stalin's offices
why: A three-aisle glass-roofed arcade on Red Square whose history tracks the entire Soviet century.

w: A drained river channel beneath an 1851 bridge became, in the chaos of the early 1990s, an open-air pawn shop for a collapsing empire: Soviet medals, cine cameras, silverware and minankari enamel jewellery still cover the asphalt. The nickname stuck once the Mtkvari river branch below was diverted for good.
s: Soviet relics spread across a drained riverbed
why: Post-Soviet economic collapse turned a 19th-century bridge into an open-air museum of everyday communism.

w: Karim Khan Zand modelled these brick-vaulted arcades on the Qeysarieh bazaar he admired in Lar, ordering construction in 1758 to make Shiraz worthy of a capital. Nineteen years and one change of dynasty later, carpet weavers, coppersmiths and spice sellers still trade beneath the same domed skylights.
s: A Zand-dynasty capital's brick-vaulted bazaar
why: Built to make 18th-century Shiraz a worthy royal capital, its vaulted brick arcades remain a working trade hub.

w: Frankincense, halwa and Omani silver have moved through this warren of lanes since dhows first worked the harbour trade, its low wooden ceilings and carved doorways barely altered by the centuries. Traders still haggle in the gloom beneath hanging lanterns a few steps from the fish quay.
s: Frankincense traded by dhow-harbour lantern light
why: One of the Arabian Peninsula's oldest working souqs, sustained for centuries by Muttrah's shipping trade.

w: Hundreds of goldsmiths line these covered lanes with windows stacked floor to ceiling in bangles, a trade that grew out of Deira's creekside dhow port decades before oil money remade the rest of the city. The wooden lattice roof still filters the same desert light onto scales weighing gold by the tola.
s: A creekside gold trade older than the oil boom
why: Deira's gold trade predates Dubai's skyline by decades, rooted in the creek's historic dhow trading port.

w: Emir Jaharkas al-Khalili razed a Fatimid caliphal mausoleum in 1382 to build this caravanserai for Cairo's merchants, and it has traded gold, spice and copperware for Mamluk, Ottoman and modern buyers ever since. Alleyways named for single trades, tentmakers, coppersmiths, still hold to their medieval guilds.
s: A 1382 caravanserai still sorted by trade guild
why: Six centuries of continuous trading on a site built over the burial ground of Cairo's Fatimid founders.

w: Snake charmers, herbalists and dye merchants have worked this open square since Marrakech's founding in 1070 as a caravan halt between the Sahara and the Mediterranean. Sacks of saffron, cumin and dried chameleons still spill from stalls once part of a trade route carrying gold and salt across the desert.
s: The medina's ancient spice and herb square
why: Sits at the historic heart of a trans-Saharan trading city founded specifically to host caravans like these.

w: Vegetable carts from the Dutch East India Company's garden gathered on this cobbled square from the 1690s, the site later serving as a slave auction ground and, from 1840, Cape Town's city hall. Craft stalls now cover cobbles once trodden by burghers, enslaved people and farmers over three centuries of trade.
s: Cobbles that saw slave sales and vegetable carts
why: One of South Africa's oldest public squares, its layered history running from VOC garden produce to slave auctions.

w: Ashanti traders sold gold dust and kola nuts here at the height of their 19th-century empire, before British colonial planners formalised the site into a market in 1924 alongside Accra's Makola. Over eight thousand stalls now spread beneath a giant circular roof, West Africa's largest single marketplace.
s: West Africa's biggest market, Ashanti-rooted
why: Grew from an Ashanti Empire trading ground into the largest single market in West Africa.

w: Sultan Ali bin Hamud commissioned this market hall in 1904, naming it after a countess connected to Zanzibar's British-era government though locals simply call it Marikiti Kuu, the main market. Spice traders, fishmongers and fruit sellers still crowd its arcades a few steps from the old slave market site.
s: Zanzibar's 1904 Sultan-built spice market
why: Built by sultanic decree in 1904, it remains Stone Town's principal produce and spice market today.

w: Merchants opened Korea's first permanent market here in 1905 to undercut royal monopoly shops and Japanese traders muscling into Jongno. Bombed flat in the Korean War and rebuilt in 1959, its bindaetteok pancake stalls and bolts of hanbok silk now draw queues through narrow, lantern-strung aisles.
s: Korea's first permanent market, since 1905
why: Founded to counter monopoly merchants and colonial trade encroachment, it is Korea's oldest surviving market.

w: Desperate Tokyoites traded rice, candy and American army surplus under these elevated Yamanote Line tracks amid the ruins of 1945, a black market that legalised into a shopping street through the 1950s. Four hundred stalls still crowd the lane, selling dried seafood, spices and cut-price sneakers.
s: A postwar black market gone respectable
why: Born from postwar food shortages as Tokyo's largest black market before legalising into today's bazaar.

w: A fish market grew up beside a temple's black gate around 1822, taking the temple's name long after the gate itself burned down in 1912. Six hundred metres of covered arcade now sell live king crab, wagyu skewers and tuna carved to order, earning the nickname Osaka's kitchen.
s: Osaka's kitchen, named for a temple's black gate
why: A temple gate long since destroyed by fire still gives its name to Osaka's premier seafood arcade.

w: Shah Jahan's daughter Jahanara laid out this market in 1650 with a canal down its centre designed to catch the moonlight, giving the street its name, Moonlight Square. Mughal processions once passed through; today jewellers, spice merchants and parantha cooks work lanes barely wider than a rickshaw.
s: A Mughal princess's moonlit market avenue
why: Designed by a Mughal emperor's daughter as a canal-lined processional route, now one of Asia's oldest markets.

w: French colonial administrators cleared two older street markets in 1889 to build this corrugated-iron hall on the edge of Hanoi's Old Quarter, its imported roof spanning 6,500 square metres. A 1994 fire gutted the stock inside; rebuilt to its original silhouette, it remains the Old Quarter's largest covered market.
s: Hanoi's largest covered market, since 1889
why: A French colonial-era market hall that survived a devastating 1994 fire to remain the Old Quarter's trading hub.

w: Buffalo pens gave this spot its Malay name, Kandang Kerbau, when cattle slaughterhouses ran here until the 1920s; Hokkien traders called it Tek Kia Kha for the bamboo along the canal. Demolished and rebuilt in 1982 as Zhujiao Market, it still trades saris, spices and mutton under its year-2000-renamed roof.
s: A buffalo-pen market renamed three times over
why: Its three successive names trace Little India's shift from cattle slaughterhouses to a wet-market landmark.

w: Royal consort Chao Dara Rasami had an old ruler's cemetery relocated in 1909 to make way for this trading site, opened the following year and named for the city's eighth ruler. Three storeys of dried chillies, fermented pork and hill-tribe textiles now trade beside its river-market twin, Ton Lamyai.
s: A market built where a royal cemetery once lay
why: Founded on relocated royal burial ground by a Chiang Mai consort, still the city's principal trading hall.

w: A public market has traded on this Front Street site since 1803, rebuilt after the Great Fire of Toronto tore through it in 1849 and expanded into twin north and south halls by 1904. Peameal bacon sandwiches and farm stalls fill a building National Geographic once ranked the world's best food market.
s: Toronto's market since before the 1849 great fire
why: In continuous operation since 1803, surviving the Great Fire of Toronto to become a National Geographic-ranked market.

w: Colonial traders arriving by canal from New Spain built this district's trade around a 1594 monastery, before the market was roofed over in 1863. Enrique del Mora's soaring 1957 modernist hall now shelters Mexico City's largest wholesale market, its dried chile and candy stalls heirs to the Aztec market of Tlatelolco.
s: Mexico City's largest market, Aztec in spirit
why: Considered the commercial heir to the great Aztec market of Tlatelolco, still the city's biggest food market.

w: Wrought iron shipped from England in 1872 raised this neoclassical fish hall beside the Mapocho river, a prefabricated frame typical of Chile's 19th-century industrial imports. Restaurateurs still arrive before dawn for congrio and Pacific shellfish beneath a glass-panelled roof that has survived earthquakes and fires.
s: English ironwork sheltering Chile's fish trade
why: A protected 1872 national monument whose imported English ironwork remains Santiago's premier seafood hub.

w: Founded in 1937 as a Chapinero market and renamed in 1946 for a burnt landmark tree, palo quemado, this hall moved to its present site near La Candelaria in 1967. Flower stalls exporting orchids worldwide sit beside fritanga cooks and fruit vendors selling lulo, pitahaya and dozens of Colombian varieties.
s: A market named for a burnt tree, since 1937
why: Bogota's benchmark flower and produce market, its odd name preserving a colonial-era landmark tree.

w: The Philadelphia and Reading Railroad tucked this market beneath its 1893 train shed after merchants refused to relocate for the new terminal, building nearly eight hundred stalls with the city's largest refrigeration plant. Amish farmers, cheesesteak counters and a donation-swallowing pig statue still fill the aisles.
s: A market tucked under a Victorian train shed
why: The last surviving 19th-century train-shed market in a city that once had several, still fully operating.

w: Fashionable Melburnians coined the phrase doing the block for promenading this stretch of Collins Street, prompting architects Twentyman and Askew to roof it in glass and mosaic between 1891 and 1893. Modelled on Milan's Galleria, its tiled floors and timber shopfronts still house a century-old tea room.
s: Where 1890s Melbourne went to 'do the block'
why: Gave rise to the Victorian-era phrase 'doing the block' and still houses an 1892 tea room in continuous operation.
